claims.text: An Mg-based alloy containing transition metals such as Ti, Zr, and Sc can be lightweight.
A two-stage 800–850 °C and 950–980 °C sintering protocol can produce a dense, single-phase-like Mg-based microstructure.
The proposed two-stage protocol will provide superior oxidation and corrosion barrier properties.
An 800–850 °C first stage will form a metastable solid solution while suppressing volatile-element loss.
A rapid 950–980 °C spike will complete densification without extensive phase segregation or volatility.
Limiting time at high temperature kinetically controls phase transformations and prevents volatility from dominating.
The starting powder consists of 99.9% Mg and Ti, Zr, and Sc powders with an average particle size below 20 µm.
Mechanical alloying of the starting powders ensures chemical homogeneity.
The first sintering stage is specified as 825 °C for 30 minutes at 5 °C/min.
The second sintering stage is specified as 975 °C for 5 minutes at 20 °C/min.
The protocol uses spark plasma sintering at 50 MPa in 99.999% argon containing less than 1 ppm oxygen.
The Stage 1 metastable solid solution acts as a precursor that suppresses segregation and volatile loss during Stage 2.
At the first-stage temperature, limited atomic diffusion favors short-range ordering and metastable solid-solution formation.
The short high-temperature stage supplies sufficient densification energy while leaving insufficient time for Mg escape or phase segregation.
The two-stage protocol will yield greater than 98% relative density and a grain size below 5 µm.
Oxidation resistance will improve by 50% relative to standard sintering.
Corrosion resistance in 3.5% NaCl will improve by 40% relative to standard sintering.
Standard sintering at 900 °C for 60 minutes produces 92% relative density, a multiphase segregated microstructure, and poor oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Below 800 °C, densification fails because diffusion is insufficient.
Above 1000 °C, Mg volatility causes elemental loss and porosity.
